power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

live_data_statements: Participants were 21 university students (M = 20.5, SD = 1.3) who had attended some form of psychotherapy in the past 2 years.
Thematic analysis was conducted to examine this heterogeneity, and to explain why participants had different priorities.
Participants were eligible if they had attended some form of psychological counselling (e.g., psychotherapy) for self-identified depressive symptoms in the past two years.
After signing up, the participants were invited on campus for individual interviews.
At the start of each study, participants provided their informed consent.
In the statement-sorting task, participants were instructed to rate the set of statements in accordance with their subjective order of importance.
Due to this fixed nature, participants were forced to assign a set amount of statements to each ranking value (e.g., only seven statements can be assigned to "neutral").
In addition, participants were asked if they feel as if there were statements relevant to their experiences that were missing.
This theme captures the variety of therapy experiences the participants had and the level of trust they had put in their therapist.
Some participants were situated in contexts that were either less supportive or lacked support.

Despite these circumstances, the participants were able to fulfil their needs for social support due to a supportive romantic partner (Luke), meaningful friendships made online (Viv), or due to supportive family members (Maya).
Towards the end of the interview, participants were asked if any relevant experiences were missing from the set of statements that have been discussed.

Some statements were ranked similarly by some participants, but for the most part, each participant had a rather distinct statement ranking with no consensus on one specific domain being the most important.
The first theme indicated that participants were able to distinguish and acknowledge which complaints were priorities and which ones were relatively minor.
Our participants indicated that such a sorting-task could be used during the intake session to point out problem areas, or throughout therapy as a way to track progress.
Many participants were inclined to see their mental health problems as something separate from their self, so that their condition did not have to define their identity, life, and goals.
A large part of participants were in late stages of adolescence at the time of their therapeutic trajectory.
Many of our participants had either already finished their therapeutic trajectory, or at the point of interviewing, had been in therapy for years.

text.text: Depression is a debilitating condition that is highly prevalent among adolescents.
However, depression is often understood through a nomothetic lens, meaning that there is a tendency to measure general patterns of symptoms.
This risks overgeneralisation that largely ignores the individual, lived experiences of depressed youth.
We develop and demonstrate a mixedmethods assessment approach in which participants can identify and elaborate on what lived experiences are important to them in therapy.
Participants were 21 university students (M = 20.5, SD = 1.3) who had attended some form of psychotherapy in the past 2 years.
Participants first performed a statement-sorting task, in which they rate the subjective importance of youth-identified experiences of depression and psychotherapy.
This task is followed by an interview on their reasons for prioritising statements.
Descriptives of the statement ratings indicated that there was a high variability in how the statements were rated.
Thematic analysis was conducted to examine this heterogeneity, and to explain why participants had different priorities.

The generated themes concerned: 1) different rationales for prioritisation of problems when navigating core problems versus "minor" problems, 2) differences in the effect of trust in the therapist on the course of therapy, 3) the degree to which one's mental health concerns are part of one's identity, and 4) if and how individuals chose to accept social support.
These findings underscore the variety in psychotherapy experiences, and suggest the need to prioritise different things in psychotherapy assessment through a tailored approach.
Adolescence is recognised as a transitional period involving a broad range of physical, cognitive, emotional, and social developmental phases.

These developmental changes coincide with an increase in psychopathology (Rapee et al., 2019), with one of the most common examples being the increased prevalence of depressive complaints (Thapar et al., 2022; World Health Organisation, 2018).

text.text: According to the DSM-5 diagnostic criteria, a patient must show at least five symptoms of depression (e.g., depressed mood most of the day, insomnia or hypersomnia nearly every day, decreased concentration nearly every day) all within a two week period.

These diagnostic criteria classify disorders with a nomothetic understanding of symptoms (Köhne, 2020), which gives little room to acknowledge the subjective experiences in disorders (Midgley et al., 2015).

text.text: In the current study, we therefore argue for a youth-tailored assessment method which systematically addresses the subjective, adolescent-specific experiences of depression.
Such an assessment method is necessary to turn the focus of assessment to what adolescents themselves indicate they need, potentially increasing the efficacy of treatment through more tailored care.
Indeed, there are several adolescent-specific factors that have been identified, which nomothetic frameworks of depressive symptoms do not account for.

Firstly, adolescents' depressive symptoms can be misattributed to regular stress or normative adolescent experiences, and are therefore not recognised as signs of depression (World Health Organisation, 2018).

text.text: Secondly, from previous studies it seems that the DSM-5 criteria for depression are not always in line with the characteristics reported by adolescents.

For example, experiences of social isolation and anger (Viduani et al., 2024), and irritability (Stringaris et al., 2013) were frequently reported among depressed adolescents, despite not being part of the DSM-5 criteria.

text.text: The other way around, there are criteria in the DSM-5 that seem less relevant for adolescents.

text.text: In this study we use a sorting task to identify relevant domains of depressive complaints and psychotherapeutic intervention from the perspectives of adolescents themselves.
Ultimately, this could be employed for a more tailored approach to the counselling of depressive complaints in youths.

We ask the main research question: "What are important experienced complaints and experiences of change in psychotherapy for adolescents with depression?", divided into two sub-questions: (1) What patterns in youth-identified complaints and experienced changes in psychotherapy can we identify?
(2) How and why do youth prioritise certain complaints/needs in psychotherapy?
We depart from existing qualitative research on adolescents' lived experiences with depression and psychotherapy to create a statement-sorting task.
We then conduct post-task interviews with the participants to capture the reasoning behind the statement's ranking, as well as the subjective context of each individual's therapeutic trajectory.

With this idiographic method, we conceptualise complaints and change within psychotherapy from the individual's experiences, potentially revealing important information about individual needs in counselling and psychotherapy.
A mixed-methods sequential design was used through several phases, as depicted in Figure 1.
text.formatted: A mixed-methods sequential design was used through several phases, as depicted in Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>.

text.text: In a first phase we synthesised qualitative literature on experiences of depression and psychotherapy of adolescents to create the statements for the sorting task.
In a second phase, the participants performed the quantitative sorting task.
In a next phase, in-depth interviews were conducted based on the sorting task results.
During the analysis, the descriptive results were used to inform what patterns/domains the in-depth qualitative analysis could focus on.

For this study's materials, existing statements were collected to create a set of statements on adolescents' lived experiences with depression and psychotherapy.
First we collected statements from an existing pilot study on adolescents in therapy for mood problems ([link to OSF page removed for peer review]).

Second, statements were collected from existing literature, which included studies implementing statement-sorting tasks and systematic reviews of qualitative studies that examined depression in adolescence (Calderon et al., 2017; Krause et al., 2021; Twivy et al., 2023; Viduani et al., 2024).

The similar statements were either combined or the copies were removed.
The merging and deletion of statements was discussed with the third author for consensus.
Afterwards, the statements were assessed by an expert on psychopathology in adolescents, who reviewed the statement content and their suitability and clarity for young participants.
The expert suggested two statements to be added, resulting in a final set of 47 statements.

text.text: Participants for this study were 21 university students between the age of 18 and 22 (M = 20.5, SD = 1.3).
Participation was compensated with university course credits.
Participants were eligible if they had attended some form of psychological counselling (e.g., psychotherapy) for self-identified depressive symptoms in the past two years.
This eligibility criterion was set to obtain a theoretically-relevant sample, based on the participants' lived experience with depressive complaints and psychotherapeutic care.
The sample size was determined by means of data saturation.
Data collection was stopped when it was assumed that recruiting additional participants would provide little additional information as the necessary depth of data was achieved.
No data was excluded from further analysis.

text.text: After signing up, the participants were invited on campus for individual interviews.
At the start of each study, participants provided their informed consent.
Afterwards, a short semistructured interview was conducted on individual's past experiences with psychotherapy.
After this introductory interview, the participants engaged in a quantitative statement-sorting task.
This task was a basis for a subsequent semi-structured interview about the participants' experiences with their complaints and psychotherapy.
In the statement-sorting task, participants were instructed to rate the set of statements in accordance with their subjective order of importance.
They were ranked in a fixed quasinormal distribution with values ranging from "least relevant, -5" to "most relevant, +5" (see
Figure 2).

text.text: Due to this fixed nature, participants were forced to assign a set amount of statements to each ranking value (e.g., only seven statements can be assigned to "neutral").
This was done to encourage thorough judgement of the importance of each statement.

The in-depth interview was conducted directly after the statement-sorting task such that the interviews could focus on what the participants found most relevant and meaningful to discuss.
The interviews were intended to gain insight into the interpretation of the statements and the rationale of the card placement on the sorting grid (Gallagher & Porock, 2010).

A pilot study was conducted with the first participants that signed up for the study (n = 8).
This pilot phase was used to examine the clarity of the initial statements and the interview guide/task instructions.
Based on the results, all of the statements were clearly understood and were left unchanged.
Slight changes were however made to the interview guide as result of the pilot phase.
Namely, some of the follow-up questions that emerged during the pilot phase were included in the general interview guide.
Inductive thematic analysis was conducted in Atlas.ti 25.0.1 (Atlas.ti Scientific Software Development GmbH, 2024).
The analysis was conducted with a contextualistic perspective.

Through this theoretical orientation, it is acknowledged that there is a certain objective reality of adolescent depression, and that individual representations (i.e., lived experiences) are influenced by the broader social context (Braun & Clarke, 2006).

text.text: The analysis was conducted by the first author, who served as the main coder, and repeatedly discussed with the third author in all stages of the analyses until consensus was reached on the final themes.
All interview transcripts were checked and read through by the first author, and preliminary insights were noted to gain familiarity with the data (phase 1).
This was followed by multiple iterations of coding the interviews for parts relevant to the research question (phase 2).
In the first iteration of coding, each interview in the dataset was coded for its semantic content.
In the second iteration of coding, more in-depth coding was performed with guidance from the quantitative findings (e.g., specific answer patterns or domains).
Codes that seemed less relevant to the research question were organised into a "rest" category.
In the third iteration, the codes were collated into higher-order codes.
These higher-order codes were organised into preliminary themes and reviewed through constant cross-examination with other codes (phase 3 & 4).

text.text: The preliminary themes were then refined and named (phase 5).
Before finalising and reporting the themes (phase 6), the codes in the "rest" category were analysed to certify that important findings have not been overlooked.
This study's research team consisted of three members who come from different epistemological backgrounds, and are at different stages within their academic trajectory.
The first author is a PhD student with a main focus on lived experiences of psychopathology in young (student) populations.
She is situated in the contextualist paradigm.
The first author primarily conducted the interviews, and at the time of interviewing, was 23 years old.
This was close in age to the participants, which may have implications for the interaction during the interviews.
Potentially, this could have fostered a more open and comfortable setting, but it could also have made the participants more uncomfortable to share certain peer-related experiences.
The second author is a full professor in computational methods in psychology, working from a primarily post-positivist paradigm.
The third author is an assistant professor in qualitative methods for youth psychotherapy, and has a constructivist epistemological stance.
This study's analysis was performed mostly through a contextualistic lens.
Throughout the study's procedure however, we have taken a pragmatic position where we used our diversity in perspectives to triangulate and interpret the data.
We first present the quantitative findings from the statement-sorting, followed by the qualitative findings from the interviews.
The quantitative findings were used to answer the sub-question: "What patterns in youth-identified complaints and experienced changes can we identify?".
The descriptive statistics indicated that there was no clear pattern in how participants sorted the statements.

Their differences in ratings signal a sample of diverse perspectives, which were used as starting point to explore the sub-question: "How and why do youth prioritise certain complaints/needs in psychotherapy?"
through inductive thematic analysis.

text.text: Based on the heterogeneous findings in the sorting task, we aimed to construe each theme as a concept that captures both the similarities as well as the divergent perspectives of said complaints and changes.
Overview of themes on experiences of complaints and change in psychotherapy for adolescents Theme 1.
Different rationales for internal prioritisation of problems: Recognising and navigating core problems versus "minor" problems in therapy
The first theme captures how the participants navigated their therapeutic priorities differently, and how this difference is reflected in their sorting task responses.
Most participants recognised the "+5" category as the core of therapy.
The category was described by participants as "the core complaints" (Paula), "the root of all problems" (Luke), and the "essentials" of therapy (Sara).
Statements that were ranked below "+5" were often recognised as more secondary, or "minor" problems.
As the participants stated, these statements were more "general everyday problems" (Lisa) or "one-off issues, not something that escalates" (Michelle).
From here on, participants diverged in their preferences/strategies for addressing these core issues versus minor issues in therapy.
We further explore this through two subthemes.
Subtheme 1A.
Addressing the "core" problems first, and "minor" problems second.
Participants expressed that they regarded the core problems as a priority, which they wanted to solve first before moving on to more minor problems.
Visualising this sorting strategy, participants would work their way from the outside (+5) towards the middle.

Michelle for example described that for her, the experience of loneliness (rated +4) was more of a background problem that she did not "actively deal with" before having worked on her issues with anxiety (rated +5).
Kylie has also stated to prioritise the resolution of the more important issues first, as the changes in primary complaints could, by association, change some of the other complaints.
Subtheme 1B.
Addressing "minor" problems first, and building up to the "core" problems.
On the other hand, there were participants that preferred to address the minor problems as a "stepping stone" (Nelly) towards the bigger complaints.
In terms of the sorting task, they would first address the statements ranked in the middle, before moving outwards to the core statements.

Beginning with these minor issues was a way for participants to build up to their primary goals, considering that the "less important" statements do influence the more important statements (e.g., for Luke).
In terms of change throughout therapy, for Valeria it was helpful to do "the little things every session" and then getting to the biggest problems.
This theme captures the variety of therapy experiences the participants had and the level of trust they had put in their therapist.
Participants reported both positive experiences and negative experiences during their therapeutic trajectory, which they stated had impacted their trust in the therapist.
Further experiences with trust in the therapist are described using three subthemes.
Subtheme 2A.
The professional role of the therapist.
Within the first subtheme, participants describe the effect of the therapist's professional role on their trust in the therapist and the state of the client-therapist relationship.
Professionality was defined through language, with Lisa reporting that the therapist's use of excessively formal language made them feel distant.
Another participant reported that the therapist's professional degree was the basis for his initial trust in therapy, though this initial trust can waver (Dennis).
This wavering trust was also noticeable from Evelin's experiences.

Her previous psychologist had shared confidential information with her parents, resulting in her being "closed off" in subsequent therapy sessions, and making it important for her to be able to trust her future therapists.
Subtheme 2B.
Actively hiding things from the therapist versus seeing no point in discussing things.

The second subtheme emphasises that participants can actively avoid mentioning certain topics in therapy, because they feel uncomfortable addressing it (e.g., Viv) or because they do not want to dedicate time to it in their sessions (Valeria).
However, participants can also avoid talking about certain topics due to a sense of anticipated failure.

The same participants for example have stated to avoid discussing their physical health due to a lack of motivation for the anticipated advice (Valeria), or to avoid discussing topics because previous advice had not worked and discussing it further seemed pointless (Viv).
Subtheme 2C.
Therapist's working style and setting.
The third subtheme describes the influence of the therapist's characteristics on the participant's trust in the therapist.
Regarding the therapist's working style, it was noted that open communication and a positive attitude was favoured (e.g., Valeria).
It was not favourable when a therapist worked inflexibly with a set step-by-step plan, especially if the plan's exercises were not helping.
Paula noted that because of this inflexibility, she did not feel as if the therapist was there to "help me with my complaints".
Participants also spoke favourably of therapy in an online setting, as this enabled them to still attend therapy with a trusted therapist when they were abroad.
For many of the participants, the domain of "identity and existence" was not regarded as something critically important to discuss during therapy.

This third theme focuses on the key reason behind this, which to our understanding is that participants draw a clear distinction between their actual self ('me as myself') and their mental health concerns ('me in therapy').
Participants recognise that mental health concerns do not have to stand in the way of personal achievements and daily life.
Maya acknowledged that whilst she had been attending therapy since childhood, she never felt directionless and always had an ambition to study psychology.
Similarly, Evelin recognised her own ambition to become a psychologist: "so I wouldn't let depression or like my mental problems get in the way of achieving the things that I want".

Participants have also noted that mental health concerns are something momentary and do not need to influence your identity: "it's just some moments of our life we experience these things, but it doesn't mean it's a part of me. […] it's really unhealthy to become your mental health issue, like make it a part of your life" (Melanie).
Other participants recognise that struggles with self-image and questioning identity were normative experiences.
For example for Maya, questioning her identity had been important during high school, but not anymore for the time being.

In another instance, Kelsey did acknowledge to struggle with her identity, however, she still saw little importance in discussing identity-related topics during therapy, as they are experiences that everyone struggles with: "who am I?
I don't know, but who does know?".
Some participants did indicate to find the domain of identity and existence important to discuss in therapy, though in this sample they were in the minority.
Charlie indicated they had always struggled with experiencing a loss in identity, and that these were mental health concerns that "actually come in the way of my life quite often".

On another note, Selena stated that she would want to resolve her negative self-image in her therapeutic trajectory, though it would be difficult to change and thus also difficult to discuss in therapy.
Many of the participants in this sample had rated the statements from the "social relationships" domain as low priority to work on or change through therapy.
The participants indicated that they knew they had a good social support system available around them (e.g., family, friends).
We understood that it was not a question of if support was available, but rather where and when it was available.
We further expand on this distinction in three subthemes.
Subtheme 4A.
Finding alternative sources of support.
Some participants were situated in contexts that were either less supportive or lacked support.

To name some experiences, Luke felt isolated from their roommates, Viv had difficulties with forming friendships outside of online contexts, and Maya felt stigmatised for their mental health concerns in their collectivistic home country.

Despite these circumstances, the participants were able to fulfil their needs for social support due to a supportive romantic partner (Luke), meaningful friendships made online (Viv), or due to supportive family members (Maya).
There seemed to be a difference between knowing that social support was available versus actually asking for social support when needed.
Participants overall acknowledged that they had supportive social relationships, and therefore did not prioritise the improvement of social relationships during therapy.
However, in some instances the participants did not reach out to others in fear of burdening them (e.g., Lisa), or in fear of opening up (e.g., Maisie), despite the support being available.
In another case, Luke felt that he did continuously have support, but he felt guilty when their support was not helpful.
In some cases, participants indicated to consciously disregard the social aspects during therapy because they did not wish to dedicate time of their therapy to social needs.
Reasons for social needs being less of an improvement point included: social needs being a "basic thing that people want"

(Gabriella) and it therefore being a lower priority; the notion that therapy should focus on the individual ("I think you're the most important person during therapy and it's not about the others"; Sara); and that in general one is not concerned with social aspects during the therapeutic trajectory (Luke).
Towards the end of the interview, participants were asked if any relevant experiences were missing from the set of statements that have been discussed.

Most participants indicated that the current statements were an accurate representation of their experiences, but almost everyone also did have additional subjective experiences they would want to add as statements.

text.text: In this study we developed a statement-sorting task and demonstrated its use in a research context.
We sought to identify relevant domains of complaints and change in psychotherapy from the perspective of youth by combining the youth-driven sorting task with in-depth qualitative interviews.

In response to the first sub-question on what patterns of complaints and change in psychotherapy can be identified, the sorting task demonstrated high heterogeneity in this sample's statement ratings.

Some statements were ranked similarly by some participants, but for the most part, each participant had a rather distinct statement ranking with no consensus on one specific domain being the most important.
As such, we did not identify patterns at group level but rather observed individualised patterns of prioritisation.

This heterogeneity suggests that there was no uniform experience of depression and change in psychotherapy, instead, there was a range of unique contexts behind the prioritisations of each individual.

The lack of consensus on these priorities is in line with previous research, which indicated that young people often report a vast range of depressive symptom experiences (Bear et al., 2021) and the developmental trajectories of such symptom experiences (Chaiton et al., 2013).

text.text: Other related work had implemented a similar statement-sorting design to examine treatment outcomes of adolescent depression (Krause et al., 2021).

text.text: In this study, participants' responses were clustered as treatment outcome profiles, yet, their analysis indicated that not all participants belonged to an outcome profile.
Similar to our verdict, clustering participants by their sorting profiles may not be "exhaustive and representative" (Krause et al., 2021, p. 314) of all viewpoints in a given sample.

text.text: Through thematic analysis, we generated four themes that contextualise the participants' sorting behaviour and their prioritisation of domains of experienced complaints and changes in psychotherapy: (1) Different rationales for internal prioritisation of problems:

Recognising and navigating core problems versus "minor" problems in therapy; (2) the importance of trust in the therapist, and how this trust affects the course of therapy; (3) recognising the boundary between 'me as myself' and 'me in therapy'; and (4) knowing where and when social support is available.

These thematic findings indicated that whilst participants differed in their priorities, there were overarching patterns in how subjective experiences have helped individuals to sort their priorities.
The first theme indicated that participants were able to distinguish and acknowledge which complaints were priorities and which ones were relatively minor.
The participants' view on the start and progression of their therapeutic trajectories diverged.
While some preferred to address the major problems first, others preferred to start with smaller problems and then progress to what they perceive as being the larger problems.

This may partially be due to differences in illness representation, which include perceptions of cause and feasibility of control of a condition (i.e., perceived chance of recovering or controlling an illness; Bear et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This may partially be due to differences in illness representation, which include perceptions of cause and feasibility of control of a condition (i.e., perceived chance of recovering or controlling an illness; <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bear et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Through these representations, individuals may also create their own perceptions of how feasible treatment and adherence is (Hagger & Orbell, 2022).
text.formatted: Through these representations, individuals may also create their own perceptions of how feasible treatment and adherence is <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Hagger & Orbell, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These findings, in turn, suggest an agency on part of the participants in prioritising complaints, which highlights the practical utility of the sorting task as therapeutic tool in clinical settings.
Our participants indicated that such a sorting-task could be used during the intake session to point out problem areas, or throughout therapy as a way to track progress.
The second through fourth theme highlight that participants can find similar domains important, due to different subjective experiences.

To illustrate, within the second theme "trust in the therapist" one individual found trust an important need because her therapist had broken the trust, whereas another individual found it important because she had experienced a positive setting with her therapist.
Recognising the different reasons participants have for prioritising trust in their therapist is important towards improving the therapeutic alliance between patient and therapist.
The therapist could for example shift their focus to how they are delivering the therapy (rather than the actual content) in cases of patients that start therapy with high mistrust (Li et al., 2022).
text.formatted: The therapist could for example shift their focus to how they are delivering the therapy (rather than the actual content) in cases of patients that start therapy with high mistrust <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Li et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast to trust in the therapist, the domain of "problems and changes in identity" was regarded as less of a priority within psychotherapy, leading to the third theme: "Recognising the boundary between 'me as myself' and 'me in therapy'".
Many participants were inclined to see their mental health problems as something separate from their self, so that their condition did not have to define their identity, life, and goals.
A large part of participants were in late stages of adolescence at the time of their therapeutic trajectory.
For them, identity formations arguably were processes that had already occurred before the start of therapy, and therefore, remained relatively stable during the therapeutic trajectory itself.
In fact, some of the participants themselves acknowledged that identity was a more important domain for them back in high school.
This could be a reason for the lack of importance assigned to identity within this study.

It would also corroborate existing research stating that identity formation processes can certainly be associated with psychopathology (Klimstra & Denissen, 2017), but that they are more central to adolescent development (Erikson, 1950).
text.formatted: It would also corroborate existing research stating that identity formation processes can certainly be associated with psychopathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Klimstra & Denissen, 2017)</ref>, but that they are more central to adolescent development <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Erikson, 1950)</ref>.

text.text: On a similar note, the fourth theme, knowing where and when social support is available, also indicated that a lack of social support was not regarded as a priority during therapy.
Existing theories indicate that depressive symptoms may serve as backdrop for interpersonal problems and vice versa (Rudolph et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Existing theories indicate that depressive symptoms may serve as backdrop for interpersonal problems and vice versa <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Rudolph et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Current findings however suggested that depressive complaints do not necessarily implicate strained interpersonal relationships, and likewise, having a supportive social context does not exclude individuals from experiencing depressive complaints.
Interestingly, our findings do indicate that individuals struggled with accepting social support, for example in the fear of burdening others, despite social support not being a key complaint.
The disparity between availability of social support and accepting the support may be an important contextual factor to consider for social adjustment (Elsina and Martinsone, 2020).
text.formatted: The disparity between availability of social support and accepting the support may be an important contextual factor to consider for social adjustment <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Elsina and Martinsone, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: For some individuals in therapy it may therefore be more appropriate to focus on accepting social support, rather than solely focusing on a lack of social support as experienced complaint.
This study details an approach to assess depressive complaints and important changes in psychotherapy, with the perspectives of adolescents as starting point.
In this section we want to address two methodological decisions.
The first decision is our sample selection.
Many of our participants had either already finished their therapeutic trajectory, or at the point of interviewing, had been in therapy for years.
Therefore they potentially were better equipped to reflect and provide rich narratives on their treatment and recovery (Henriksen, 2014).
text.formatted: Therefore they potentially were better equipped to reflect and provide rich narratives on their treatment and recovery <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Henriksen, 2014</ref>).

text.text: Yet, it could have also been a limitation to rely on the participants' reflections only, as it could overlook important insights held during therapy.
Future research could therefore examine adolescents' experiences of depression prospectively or during the therapeutic trajectory.
Using this study's sorting task to map their experiences could deliver interesting complementary results to the current findings.
The second decision to discuss is the use of a mixed-methods approach.

The mixedmethods approach allowed for a novel structured and in-depth examination of experienced complaints and changes in psychotherapy, which would have not been possible through a quantitative or qualitative approach only.

We note that such an assessment can be quite resource-intensive for the researcher and/or practitioner to utilise, especially in combination with other professional activities (Gürsoy & Vatansever, 2025).
text.formatted: We note that such an assessment can be quite resource-intensive for the researcher and/or practitioner to utilise, especially in combination with other professional activities <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Gürsoy & Vatansever, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Despite the associated time and labour intensity, it remains important to consider such qualitative designs as the groundwork for idiographic assessment.

Qualitative components are key to uncovering new perspectives (Gürsoy & Vatansever, 2025), and they are especially complementary to more quantitative methods when examining complex mental health problems (Demkowicz et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Qualitative components are key to uncovering new perspectives <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Gürsoy & Vatansever, 2025)</ref>, and they are especially complementary to more quantitative methods when examining complex mental health problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Demkowicz et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This specific assessment method is an accessible task to administer to adolescents, it can for example help adolescents visualise and identify the experiences and complaints they struggle with.
For researchers, such a sorting task can be used to provide a justification for what should be measured, and why (Bringmann et al., 2022).
text.formatted: For researchers, such a sorting task can be used to provide a justification for what should be measured, and why <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bringmann et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The sorting task plus interview could help towards improving design choices by justifying the domains and constructs of interest.
One timely application being Experience Sampling Methodology.

For practitioners, it may be fruitful to include such a sorting task throughout the therapeutic process for shared decision-making on the content of therapy sessions, or to decide which topics should be emphasised/which topics are less relevant.
Such interaction may foster patient-therapist collaborations and co-creation in psychotherapy.
Our study provides a means to map heterogeneity in, and subjective experiences of depression and psychotherapy during adolescence.

These findings highlight the importance of taking subjectivity of experiences into account during interventions, as subjective experiences can reveal a lot of important information about person-specific needs.
Utilising such an assessment method can therefore inform more tailored care of depressive complaints.
